title: Antecedents and correlates of improved cognitive performance in children exposed in utero to low levels of lead.
ehr_evidence: Capillary blood samples were collected when the children were 6, 12, 18, and 24 months old and venous samples when they were 57 months old. Data were collected prospectively for this research study, not from routine clinical records.
summary: Prospective longitudinal cohort study examining cognitive recovery between 24 and 57 months in children with varying prenatal and postnatal lead exposures, finding that higher prenatal exposure predicts greater relative improvement, moderated by postnatal lead levels and sociodemographic factors.
key_findings: Higher prenatal lead exposure (cord blood) was associated with greater relative cognitive improvement between 24 and 57 months (beta=0.03, p=0.016 adjusted).
Postnatal blood lead levels at 18, 24, and 57 months were inversely associated with cognitive improvement (e.g., 24-month level: beta=-0.22, p=0.005 adjusted).
Among children with high prenatal exposure, girls showed significantly greater cognitive improvement than boys (difference of 7.7 points, p=0.017).
Higher HOME scores, social class, maternal IQ, and older maternal age were associated with greater cognitive improvement.
No significant association was found between cognitive improvement and ethnicity (p=0.57 adjusted).
data_source_type: prospective research cohort with direct data collection
population: children followed from birth, assessed at 24 and 57 months (n=170 at 57 months)
limitations: restricted range of prenatal exposures in low/medium groups
cognitive tests measure different skills at different ages
